```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  fig.width = 7,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

**spatialising** simulates changes in binary spatial patterns using two main pressures: the external pressure `B` and the local interaction strength `J`.
Positive values of `B` favor class `1`, negative values favor class `-1`, and larger absolute values have a stronger effect across the pattern.
Larger values of `J` make neighboring cells more likely to have the same class, creating larger patches and reducing isolated cells.

By default, `B` is constant across all cells, but `external_field` allows a different adjustment for each cell, for example based on a spatial probability map.
At cell $i$, the effective external pressure is then $B + \mathtt{external\_field}_i$.
Let's see that on an example.

## Probability map

We use the 2013 Maine forest pattern as the initial state and the 2016 pattern as a visual reference.
The 2016 pattern is not used to create the probability map or choose the simulation parameters.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(terra)
library(spatialising)

maine2013 = rast(system.file("raster/maine2013.tif", package = "spatialising"))
maine2016 = rast(system.file("raster/maine2016.tif", package = "spatialising"))
```

Moreover, we have a probability map `p` that represents the probability of each cell being class `1`.

```{r}
p = rast(system.file("raster/maine_probability.tif", package = "spatialising"))
```

In this example, the probability map is based only on the 2013 pattern and assumes that most cells keep their original class.^[But in practice, the probability map could be based on other spatial variables, such as elevation, distance to roads, or other environmental factors; or it could be a prediction from a machine learning model.]
We assume that cells at class boundaries are more likely to change than cells inside larger patches -- so the boundary cells were given a 25% chance of changing class, compared with 5% for other cells.
Because `p` is the probability of class `1`, its possible values are 0.05, 0.25, 0.75, and 0.95.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.5
names(maine2013) = "2013"
names(p) = "Probability of class 1"
names(maine2016) = "2016"
plot(c(maine2013, p, maine2016), nr = 1)
```

## Simulation

The `external_field` argument of `kinetic_ising()` allows to use a spatially varying external pressure.
Its values are in the same units as `B`, so we need to convert the probabilities in `p` to the pressure scale.
To do that, we use the log-odds transformation.
We set `B = 0`, so the effective external pressure is just the log-odds of the probability of class `1`:

```{r}
B = 0
external_field = 0.5 * log(p / (1 - p)) - B
```

The value `J = 0.3` (local interaction strength) is chosen only for this illustration.
Using the same random seed makes it easier to compare the effect of the spatial field.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
without_field = kinetic_ising(maine2013, B = B, J = 0.3)

set.seed(1)
with_field = kinetic_ising(maine2013, B = B, J = 0.3, external_field = external_field)
```

Compared with using `B = 0` alone, the field makes core cells less likely to change while allowing more change at class boundaries.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.5
names(without_field) = "Without external field"
names(with_field) = "With external field"
plot(c(without_field, with_field), nr = 1)
```
